data.title: Trump is hitting the campaign trail. But he's largely missing from GOP ads.
data.description:
Trump is hitting the campaign trail. But he's missing from GOP ads.

Jessica Piper, Jason Beeferman and Meredith Lee Hill
Updated Sat, October 17, 2026 at 2:00 PM UTC
7 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Donald Trump is barnstorming the country to boost Republicans in the final weeks of the midterms. But many candidates want to keep that support quiet.

The president is nowhere to be found in GOP ads, even in red states where Republicans were happy to tout his endorsement two years ago. And some candidates are hesitant to appear with Trump on the campaign trail — even as they hope he will help juice turnout among the MAGA base in November.

Democratic House and Senate candidates and outside groups have spent $145 million on general election ads mentioning Trump, while Republicans have spent just $8 million, according to a POLITICO analysis of data from AdImpact, which tracks political advertising. That's in sharp contrast to 2024, when GOP candidates spent $62 million on ads mentioning Trump.

Advertisement

"Trump is at historic lows right now, so if he comes to your district or state, it's about getting the Republican base vote out there and that can certainly help," said Ron Bonjean, a longtime GOP strategist. "But it's really important for the candidates not to be talking about Trump 24/7 on the campaign trail."

The unfavorable national political environment leaves few incentives for GOP candidates to tie themselves to Trump, and more and more Republicans in competitive races have broken with the president on issues such as the Iran war and tariffs.

When Republicans do mention Trump in ads, they often aren't touting his support. In Alaska, GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan has run an ad citing how he "voted to force Trump's DOJ to release the Epstein files."

The silence on the airwaves is especially stark in red states like Nebraska and Ohio. In 2024, Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.), who was facing a challenge from independent Dan Osborn, and now-Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), who was challenging then-Sen. Sherrod Brown, both ran several general election ads featuring endorsements from Trump. The president won Nebraska by more than 20 points and Ohio by 12 points that year, with Fischer and Moreno also winning their races.

But this cycle, the GOP isn't focusing its ads on Trump in either state, as the match-up between Osborn and Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts heats up in Nebraska and Brown seeks to oust Republican Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio.

Both Ricketts and Husted appeared at Trump rallies earlier this month. Still, Trump is absent from all Republican Senate ads in Ohio, and the only Ricketts ads that name the president accuse Osborn of disparaging Trump supporters — but don't mention Trump's endorsement.

"The war in Iran, I think, has become a real noose around the neck of Republican candidates because of the affordability crisis," said former Ohio Rep. Jim Renacci. A nonprofit he works with surveyed voters on whether GOP candidates should appear with Trump and found that "in most cases you do not want [Trump] standing near you, which is why I was a little bit surprised that Jon Husted has had two events with President Trump, because I do believe there's a strong headwind in Ohio, and a big change from 2024."

Husted's campaign spokesperson Amy Natoce told POLITICO in a statement, "President Trump won Ohio decisively three times by 8 points, 8 points and 11 points. If we successfully turn out the MAGA vote this November, then we will retire Sherrod Brown for good."

The National Republican Senatorial Committee did not respond to a request for comment.

"President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said. "The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump's winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats' extreme liberal policies and obstruction."

Another Republican operative, who is based in Ohio and like others was granted anonymity to speak candidly about their own party, said GOP candidates need to find a way to talk about the Trump administration — no tax on tips, protecting social security — without mentioning the guy in the Oval Office.

"This is a historically unpopular president," said the strategist, who has worked on multiple statewide races over the course of the last 15 years. "We all agree with that, and so it's kind of hard to attach yourself on the airways, I think, too closely to him."

Trump's rallies, unlike candidates' ads, are seen more as targeting the president's base. He's not only visiting traditional battlegrounds like Georgia and Michigan, but also typically safe red states like Alabama and Kansas.

Still, his events have been a source of tension with some GOP candidates. When Trump's team was making plans for the president to campaign in Michigan last week potentially in western Michigan, several Republican candidates and their teams up and down the ticket initially didn't know whether they should attend and be seen with the president, according to three Republicans with direct knowledge of the conversations, who were granted anonymity to share private details. They were concerned about being associated with Trump's tariffs, which have hammered the state, along with high fuel prices amid the Iran war.

Trump officials scrapped the event and said the president would visit the state later in the month. Trump is now scheduled for a rally in the state on Oct. 25.

"[Republican candidates] are going to do what they need to do," said one GOP pollster close to the White House. "What the White House and the president are doing is they are targeting places where they think the president can be helpful."

Trump has allowed Republicans to discuss issues pertaining to their states or districts as "he understands that it is not a balk on him," said one White House official, granted anonymity to speak candidly.

If Trump "was to believe that all these individuals were balking him, I A) don't think that he would want to be on the road every day, and B) I do think that you would probably see a more vocal President Donald J. Trump on Truth, et cetera, kind of voicing his opinion on it," the official said.

The president and his team are giving most Senate GOP candidates especially a wide latitude to break with some of his policies at times, according to two other White House officials involved in the conversations. Trump, they said, understands the need for vulnerable candidates to create some distance, even though in the past he has lashed out at members of his party for similar moves.

Republicans in the more MAGA-friendly House, however, are expected to run more in lock-step with the president. Only the most at-risk candidates are afforded some room to break with Trump, the officials said, given the tidal wave of chaos that can spur within the conference.

One GOP strategist working on a battleground House race, granted anonymity to discuss private information, said he had gotten pre-approved from the White House for his candidate to miss a planned rally. Still, the strategist cautioned, that doesn't mean Trump won't berate someone from the stage when he notices the candidate is missing.

Republicans still see Trump as a unique motivator for his base and rallies as a tool to help turn out voters who might be driven by the president. With Democratic voters already energized by opposing Trump, the GOP has less to lose by bringing the president out to turn out MAGA voters too.

"The reality is, Democrats are going to vote in this midterm," said Paul Shumaker, a Republican strategist from North Carolina, where Trump is set to return for a rally next week as GOP Senate nominee Michael Whatley struggles to close the gap in his race. "And what Republicans need to be doing is focus on what they can do to improve their voter turnout on their side."

Lauren Fedor, Myah Ward, Andrew Howard and Alex Gangitano contributed to this report.

data.title: Zelensky urges support for new U.S. sanctions on Russia after Trump puts them on hold
data.description:
Zelenskyy urges support for new US sanctions on Russia after Trump puts them on hold

Associated Press
Updated Sat, October 17, 2026 at 10:11 AM UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged supporters Saturday to speak out in defense of new U.S. sanctions against Russia, hours after President Donald Trump signed an executive order pausing a sweeping package of restrictions targeting the Russian economy.

The White House decision has further raised fears that Ukraine could be left exposed to Moscow's escalating assaults with winter approaching.

Russian attacks overnight killed at least four people, including an ambulance driver, and injured dozens, officials said. Ukrainian drones killed a woman in a Russian border region and disrupted flights at Moscow's airports, according to Russian authorities.

Advertisement

Zelenskyy described Trump's move to put sanctions on hold as unfortunate, but did not directly criticize the U.S. leader despite deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington in recent days.

"A decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Zelenskyy wrote.

He also expressed hope that the new sanctions could be revived. "This Act could have helped enormously — and still can! But it needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters," he said.

Critics say Trump's decision helps Putin

Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling Russia's 4 1/2-year-old war against Ukraine. The bill had sought to sanction Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.

Trump personally signed the legislation just last month and his move came just two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation. The President told Congress that the pause was in the national interest but gave no further details.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who co-drafted the bill, said in a statement that Trump was turning his back on "the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies."

"These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin," Blumenthal said.

Trump's unexpected decision comes a week after he stunningly said the U.S. had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia.

Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."

The decision has been pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike who say it will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine -- without making a difference to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump's war on Iran.

Kyiv says Moscow carried out a 'massive' energy strike

Zelenskyy also said Saturday that Moscow had carried out a massive strike on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, targeting more than 15 sites across the country.

"The sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia's strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences," he said.

Ukraine's air force said that Russian forces launched four cruise missiles and 332 attack drones overnight. All of the missiles and 289 of the drones had been suppressed or destroyed, it said.

Russia's heavy bombardment of the power grid ahead of winter has been an annual feature of the war, aimed at wearing down Ukraine's appetite for the fight by denying civilians heat and running water. Ukrainian officials have warned that Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles for more attacks in the coming months.

Russian attacks killed three people in the Ukrainian city of Sloviansk, Vadym Liakh, head of the city military administration, said Saturday. Writing on social media, Liakh said that two apartment blocks were partially destroyed and other homes damaged.

A Russian strike also killed an ambulance driver in Ukraine's Kherson region, head of the local military administration Yaroslav Shanko said. The strike, which used guided bombs, injured at least 33 others, he said.

Ukrainian drones kill 1, ground hundreds of flights at Moscow airports

Elsewhere, a Russian woman was killed in a Ukrainian drone attack in the Russian border region of Belgorod, local officials said.

Russia's Ministry of Defense said Saturday that its forces had shot down 610 Ukrainian drones overnight over 15 Russian regions, as well as the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that more than 100 drones were shot down en route to the Russian capital. More than 350 flights were canceled or delayed at Moscow's airports, local media reported, as planes were grounded in response to incoming drones.

The Kremlin announced Saturday that Russian President Vladimir Putin had approved a government program to help restore trade and logistics facilities damaged in drone attacks.

data.title: An armed dad and a teacher stopped an Oregon school shooter. It took just 3 minutes.
data.description:
See all topics
Email
Link Copied!

On a sunny Oregon fall morning, parents dressed their children up and sent them to Silver Rail Elementary School for picture day. It’s the kind of picture parents return to years later, marveling at how small their children once were and how their smiles looked before their faces changed.

But for some families, snapshots in their minds from that morning will carry a devastating, final memory of a child who never came home.

Just hours after Steven and Angela Nuchols sent their 8-year-old daughter to school, they raced back to Silver Rail, desperate to know whether she was alive, they told local news outlet, The Bend Source.

“It was crawling with police officers from all over the county,” Angela Nuchols told The Bend Source. “You’ve got guys in tactical gear, rifles. You’re just scared to death wondering, is your child OK?”

For the Nuchols family, the next few hours before they were reunited with their daughter at a church were “the worst three hours of our lives,” Angela said.

American schools have repeatedly seen the illusion of safety shattered within the walls of their classrooms. An elementary school in Bend, Oregon, was the latest among them, when a 16-year-old opened fire on Thursday, killing three children, including Rhoam Summer, aged 5; and two others, aged 8 and 11; as well as a 25-year-old teacher, Megan Lambert, police said. A 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were injured and taken to local hospitals, according to officials.

Another school turned into a crime scene; a violation of the sanctity of childhood.

A drone view shows Silver Rail Elementary School, the day after a shooting, in Bend, Oregon, October 16.

180 seconds of terror

Michelle was a freshman in high school in California when she survived a school shooting in 2001. The trauma followed her into adulthood; she learned to scan rooms for exits, sit facing doors and live with anxiety and panic attacks.

Long before the shooting, every school drop-off carried a quiet dread. Michelle, who is withholding her last name for privacy, would watch her children go, a pit in her stomach, wondering whether she would see them again.

Then, on Thursday, her fifth-grade son called from Silver Rail Elementary School.

“Mom, there’s a shooter.”

Michelle was eating at an Olive Garden when her son’s voice came through his Apple Watch. She cried while recounting the moment, and said she immediately knew from the sound of his voice that something was terribly wrong.

She told him she loved him, urged him to stay quiet and hung up to call 911. As she ran to her car, the call rang without an answer. She raced toward the school, about 10 minutes away.

“I was like, how can this happen?” Michelle wonders, her voice shaking. “How can lightning strike twice?”

A mother who lived through a 2001 school shooting comforts her son during Silver Rail Elementary shooting.

The first 911 call came at 12:59 p.m., after the driver of a red pickup truck saw a man approach the school, throw his long gun over the fence and climb over after it, police said Friday. When the pickup driver confronted him, the suspect opened fire, striking the truck at least three times.

From her classroom window, fifth-grade teacher Kathy Sheil Smith watched the gunman walk toward the building. She called the main office, then pulled her students into a corner.

“They were so afraid. The looks on their faces, it was really hard to see,” Sheil Smith told CNN affiliate KPTV, trying to hold back tears. “Some kids were praying, some kids were consoling other kids. But they were doing so quietly because they know you don’t make any noise.”

She wondered whether she would live to see the end of the day. What mattered to her was that her students would.

“I’m sure that every teacher at the school thought, ‘Today is the day that I am going to die,’” Sheil Smith told CNN affiliate KPTV. “Save my kids.”

As Smith tried to shield her students inside the school, a terrifying picture was emerging. Around 12:59 p.m., emergency dispatchers received a flood of calls reporting that a person had entered the Silver Rail Elementary School and started shooting, according to Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz. At 1:01 p.m., police directed the school to go into lockdown.

“Ms. Hawkins, the principal, was saying ‘lockdown, lockdown,’ and then the shots kept on going and going,” one 9-year-old student told CNN affiliate KGW, describing how he hid under a sink for 30 minutes, fearing the gunman would approach his classroom next.

“I’m pretty sure a girl. She was saying, ‘Please, please, no,’ and then it was a shot and then dead silence,” he added.

The gunman went directly into the classroom just left of the entrance and fired as many as 15 rounds, according to Krantz. The classroom was dedicated to special needs students, according to Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook.

A second driver, a 36-year-old father whose children attend the school, had witnessed the initial shooting, drove into the school parking lot and followed the suspect into the school with his legally secured 40-caliber pistol, police said. The bystander was identified by his family as Kaylub Giamanco on Friday.

A teacher — who was not injured — threw her cellphone at the shooter and tackled him in an attempt to get the gun away from him, the police chief said. When Giamanco heard gunfire and saw the teacher physically struggling with the gunman, Giamanco entered the classroom and fired, striking the suspect multiple times and killing him, police said.

Less than half a mile away, business owner Sierra Jordan told CNN the familiar sound of children laughing and playing outside at recess gave way to the frantic arrival of ambulances.

About three minutes after the first 911 call, it was over: At 1:02 p.m., police arrived and reported the shooter had been shot and killed by Giamanco. President Donald Trump called Giamanco “a great hero” who “took care of business.”

“Had this not happened, had the bystander not neutralized the shooter? This could have been a much more tragic event than it was,” former FBI special agent Ken Gray told CNN.

The shooter was identified as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, a former special needs student at the school, Krantz said Friday. A Maverick 88 pump-action, 12-gauge shotgun was found near the suspect, who had about 44 remaining rounds of 12-gauge ammunition, Krantz added.

The gun had been purchased by his mother, a senior law enforcement official briefed on the investigation told CNN earlier Friday.

Tragedy plunges community into grief

Bend, a picturesque city of about 100,000 people, sits in the high desert landscape of central Oregon. It is a city of sage-scented air, snow-capped peaks and the Deschutes River that cuts through the heart of downtown; a magnet for thrill-seekers finding solace in the nearby mountain trails, red rock cliffs and star-filled skies.

Although the city has boomed in recent years, it remains a quiet corner of the American West where the wilderness begins just beyond the city streets and its brick front stores and breweries.

“Bend is a place that people move to from bigger cities,” Former Bend Mayor Jeff Eager told CNN. “They move here because it’s relatively safe here; they move here because we have schools you can walk your kids to,” Eager said. “You can’t imagine that it happens here.”

But against Bend’s picturesque backdrop, the aftermath looked devastatingly familiar. Parents rushing to a reunification center, hearts clenched with the hope of finding their children among the survivors. Police tape cordoned off the school as officers stood guard.

An emergency worker holds up police tape at the scene of a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, October 15.

The minutes had passed so quickly for the rest of the world, but for the families waiting to learn whether their children were alive, the abrupt end of the gunfire wasn’t the end of their agony.

The prevalence of school shootings in America should prompt a conversation about “responsible gun ownership,” Democratic Rep. Janelle Bynum of Oregon told CNN.

“This school, we had invested money in to make sure that it was locked. They did all of their drills as expected — everything that we’ve said that will protect kids up to now, and yet it didn’t work,” she said.

“The laws don’t go far enough, fast enough for us to be able to intervene,” Bynum said.

“We have to stop allowing our children to be shredded in schools, grocery stores, parks, churches. We have to stop this violence.”

Investigators seek answers

The Bend-La Pine school district — of which Silver Rail Elementary School is part — has multiple security measures in place such as secure entry vestibules, photo ID checks and visitor screenings, indoor and outdoor security cameras and upgraded locks on classroom doors that can be secured from inside, according to the district.

Despite those measures, some of which were upgraded in 2022, the gunman was able to force his way into the elementary school by shooting at locked doors.

It is not yet clear why the shooter was able to bypass security measures, the district’s superintendent said.

Related article
The sun rises over downtown Roseburg, Oregon, inside the Umpqua Valley.

Shadows in the valley: Nearly eight years after a shooting at Umpqua Community College left nine people dead, an Oregon community is still trying to heal

14 min read

Investigators are still working to establish a motive for the shooting, authorities said Friday.

A search warrant was executed at the alleged shooter’s house on Thursday, according to a senior law enforcement official, who told CNN computers and other electronics were taken. Search warrants have also been obtained to gain access to the devices and extract data, according to the source.

Local law enforcement and the FBI will examine the material for evidence that could help explain what led to the shooting. The shooter’s parents were cooperative and told investigators their son had attended Silver Rail Elementary School during their interview, the source said.

During the pandemic, the shooter’s mother spoke with CNN affiliate KTVZ about her hopes that in-person classes would resume for children with special needs. The program was described as serving children with “intensive behavioral and social skills challenges.”

She spoke briefly with CNN off camera from her balcony on Friday but declined to comment on how her son got access to the weapon. Authorities say that is still under investigation. The woman told CNN there were no warning signs.

“I miss my boy. I’m so sorry,” the woman said as she cried and smoked a cigarette.

In a message to the families of those killed, she said: “I’m so sorry, I wish I could have done something. I’m sorry for their loss.”

Another chorus of thoughts and prayers

Members of the Bend community gathered downtown in Drake Park on Thursday evening for a prayer vigil to support each other and grieve. Bend Mayor Melanie Kebler spoke while in tears alongside Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek, who was also crying.

A large crowd of mourners held candles and hugged one another as they listened to prayers, music and community leaders. People wrote tributes in chalk. “NEVER again,” one person wrote. “Be at peace,” scribbled another. A young child knelt to place a lit candle on a step.

By Friday, a makeshift memorial had taken shape outside Silver Rail Elementary School. Bouquets of flowers, toys and red, heart-shaped balloons lined a nearby crosswalk, just beyond yellow police tape.

One mother, Ally Land, brought her children, 8 and 5, to the memorial. Her children don’t attend Silver Rail, but Land said she wanted to help them understand what had happened, answering their questions as best she could.

“I asked them what they knew, and they just said, ‘I know that school’s canceled, so that they can make school safer tomorrow,’” Land told CNN. “We told them something terrible had happened, and we just followed their questions from there.”

All Bend-La Pine Schools were closed on Friday, including activities and athletic events, the district said.

But a day without classes cannot prevent the next shooting.

The Silver Rail Elementary tragedy is the 36th shooting in the United States this year on K-12 school grounds, according to CNN’s analysis of multiple databases, including the Gun Violence Archive.

“As a country, we still lack the courage to do anything to try to prevent these things from occurring,” CNN’s Senior Law Enforcement Analyst Charles Ramsey told CNN’s Elex Michaelson on Friday. “And it’s going to happen again.”

Blake and Danielle Brinker were at their home outside Bend with Blake’s mother when they learned of the shooting, they told CNN. Blake said, describing his emotions at the time, as “just absolutely gutted.” The pair, who know people directly affected by the shooting, also visited the memorial.

“Immediately could feel the energy of the community just stop on a dime,” Blake said.

Danielle described Bend as “a very magical place.”

A woman lights a candle during a candlelight vigil at Drake Park for victims of the Silver Rail Elementary School shooting, in Bend, Oregon, October 15.

The town was named in the top 75 safest midsize cities in the country, according to a SmartAsset study earlier this year. But Thursday’s deadly shooting isn’t the first in Bend. In 2022, a 20-year-old gunman, a Bend resident, killed two people after walking into a grocery store with an AR-15-style rifle and opening fire.

Back in Bend, Cook, the district superintendent at Bend-La Pine Schools, spent Friday with staff at the school who are grappling with the devastating aftermath.

“They are in so much pain, as we all are,” Cook said. “This has been a terrifying and traumatic experience that will affect us all profoundly for years to come.”

Michelle, the 2001 school shooting survivor and a mother of children at Silver Rail Elementary School, carried for years the knowledge that gun violence could shatter an ordinary day without warning. But she’d hoped her children would never have to know what that’s like.

“My friend said to me, this is generational trauma, this is a second generation that’s been through school shooting trauma,” Michelle told CNN. “How sick is that?”

CNN’s Taylor Galgano, Helen Regan, Emma Tucker, Norma Galeana, Caroll Alvarado, Alisha Ebrahimji, Amanda Jackson, Leigh Waldman, John Miller, Rebekah Riess and Elise Hammond contributed to this report.

data.title: U.S. deficit nears $2 trillion as government spending keeps climbing
data.description:
The US federal budget deficit for 2026 just came in. It's $1.992 trillion.

Ben Werschkul · Washington Correspondent
Fri, October 16, 2026 at 2:19 PM CDT 4 min read

The US federal budget deficit for 2026 officially came in Friday at $1.992 trillion, a final tabulation to close out the government's fiscal year and another reminder of Washington's spiraling reliance on red ink.

This deficit number represents about 6% of the US gross domestic product and was a result of $5.403 trillion in total revenues for the fiscal year against total spending of $7.396 trillion.

The 2026 reading is a 12% jump from 2025's $1.775 trillion deficit.

These final numbers came in the Treasury Department's Monthly Statement for September, which covers the final month in the US government's fiscal calendar.

The red ink has led to dire warnings from economists that the US now routinely runs annual deficits that were previously seen only during recessions and wars. The gross US national debt passed $40 trillion in August and now sits above $40.3 trillion.

The latest "Debt to the Penny" reading from the Treasury Department came this past Wednesday, putting the gross US national debt at $40,329,229,827,541.02.

Read more: How the soaring federal debt affects you personally

The independent budget hawks at the Committee for a Responsible Budget noted in a recent analysis that "the country's future fiscal outlook is even more dismal," noting that annual deficits could reach $3.1 trillion by 2036 without a change in the fiscal trajectory.

The group noted that annual interest costs on the debt are now $1.1 trillion, a record 3.4% of GDP, making it the second-largest line item in the government's budget. Interest on the debt still costs less than Social Security, but it is now more expensive than either Medicare or the defense budget.

Members of President Trump's team have tried to downplay this year's tabulation — the highest annual deficit reading other than 2020 and 2021, when budgets were inflated by COVID-era spending — as a blip and insist that the US fiscal situation is getting under control.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has focused on the Supreme Court-ordered tariff refunds that have turned a revenue stream into a cost center for the government in recent months.

Indeed, the impact of tariff refunds has been significant: $144.6 billion in tariff refunds were given out over the past year — but analyses of the deficit also show a variety of factors that have driven up deficits.

A Hamilton Project tracker of government expenditures shows how government spending has increased at a steady pace in 2026. The tracker looks at spending by calendar year and shows that as of Oct. 14, government spending has jumped each of the last three years.

At this point in 2024 — the last year of Joe Biden's presidency — the government had spent $5.76 trillion. On Oct. 14, 2025, spending had grown to $6.13 trillion. So far this year, the government has spent $6.65 trillion.

One of the drivers, a Bloomberg Government analysis found, is spending on Trump administration priorities, especially the Department of Homeland Security, whose budget is up 146% from 2025 to 2026.

Revenue downturn

The revenue side of the US government's budget equation has also faltered on some fronts in 2026, in part due to tax cuts implemented by Trump's "One Big Beautiful Bill."

A monthly budget review from the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) released last week noted that tariff revenues declined, as did corporate income tax collections.

The group calculates that corporate income taxes decreased by 16% in 2026 as the new tax cuts allowed corporations to take larger deductions "and offset the increases in those receipts that otherwise would have been expected, given the rise in corporate income."

Tariffs were also a significant factor, with the Supreme Court's decision in February striking down Trump's tariffs leading to a refund process in the months that followed that has made tariffs barely a profitable undertaking for the government in 2026.

The $144.6 billion in tariff refunds nearly halved the gross receipts of $317.8 billion. And at least some additional tariff refunds could be seen in the months ahead, with the government recently launching "Phase 3" of the refund process.

This turnabout in tariffs led to a deficit approximately $140 billion higher than projections from just a few months ago. In February, before the tariff refunds were ordered, the CBO projected a $1.85 trillion annual deficit for this year.

Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance.

data.title: Trump pauses Russia sanctions passed by Congress, citing U.S. national interest
data.description:
Trump puts new Russia sanctions passed by Congress on hold, saying waiver is in US national interest

WILL WEISSERT and MEG KINNARD
Updated Sat, October 17, 2026 at 1:42 AM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order that puts on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause was in the national interest.

Trump had signed the legislation last month. Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, the measure had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling the war against Ukraine.

The move comes a week after Trump stunningly said the U.S. had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try and bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia.

Advertisement

The Trump administration has remained mostly quiet since the recent passage of the bill with large bipartisan majorities in the House and Senate after Graham's sudden death — with lawmakers urged ahead by Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Trump's latest action followed the president announcing on social media last week that he had reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he was expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia.

Instead, Trump announced that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.

The measure also had become a campaign centerpiece for Sen. Darline Graham, the late senator's sister appointed to serve out the remaining months in his current term, who is also running to replace him in the Senate more permanently.

In a debate earlier this week with Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, Graham — who has Trump's endorsement and is expected to campaign with him in South Carolina next week — said she had been "so proud" to help get the measure passed but acknowledged it was the president's purview as to how he implemented it.

"It gives the president tools that he can use if he so chooses, to end the war through economic sanctions," Graham said Sunday during a debate in Columbia. "So that's up to him as to whether or not he wants to use it, or whether he wants to use something else, but I think the purpose of it is to bring down the gas prices and ultimately end the war. And when the war ends, gas prices will fall."

data.title: A teacher saved lives by tackling and fighting the Oregon shooter, police say
data.description:
Teacher and armed parent teamed up to stop Oregon school shooter, police say

By Herbert Villarraga and Deborah Bloom
Sat, October 17, 2026 at 1:17 AM UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Herbert Villarraga and Deborah Bloom

BEND, Oregon, Oct 16 (Reuters) - A 16-year-old boy who shot and killed a teacher and three children in an Oregon special-needs classroom was stopped by another teacher who tackled him and an armed father who fatally shot him, officials said on Friday.

Their actions on Thursday ‌saved other lives, the local police chief told a press conference.

A day into their investigation of the latest US school shooting, police released new details of the ‌scene at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, where three schoolchildren aged 5, 8 and 11 were killed along with 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert.

Advertisement

A 7-year-old was wounded and listed in serious but stable condition, and another ​teacher suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries, police said.

The unidentified teacher who stopped the shooter on Thursday threw her phone at him, tackled and fought him. A 36-year-old father of two students then rushed in with a legal .40-caliber pistol and fired at the suspect multiple times, killing him just before police arrived.

This teacher, who was not injured, "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz, at times choking back emotion, told a press conference.

"The teacher who was willing to stand and fight for her children, that's true heroism," he said, without identifying her.

Kenda Freeman told ‌the New York Times that her son Kaylub Giamanco, whose two ⁠daughters attend the school, killed the shooter, according to video posted by the New York Times of Freeman reading a brief statement.

"He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and ⁠support," Freeman said, adding that he asked for privacy and did not want to speak to the media.

Officials identified the shooter as Griffin J. John II, a 16-year-old former special-needs student at the school who was armed with a 12-gauge shotgun. He fired about 15 rounds in the classroom and had another 44 rounds on him, police said.

Police were trying to determine what motivated the shooter and how he ​obtained ​a Maverick 88 pump-action 12-gauge shotgun, Krantz said.

"Everyone wants to know why, including us ... We may never ​get that full answer, but we want it," the police chief said.

Just ‌before the shooting, the assailant was seen throwing his weapon over the school fence and then climbing after it onto school grounds. The driver of a truck passing by at the time verbally confronted the boy, who opened fire on the vehicle.

The assailant shot through locked glass doors and stormed a class of mixed-grade special-needs students. Police arrived within three minutes of the first call, and the shooter was already dead, Krantz said.

VICTIMS MOURNED

People in Bend, a city of about 100,000 some 175 miles (280 km) southeast of Portland, gathered near the school to mourn on Friday morning, placing flowers and candles outside yellow crime scene tape that cordoned off the scene.

"Thank God for that father," Michael Zappa, 71, who lives just ‌blocks from the school, said through tears. "He saved a lot of lives yesterday, and our prayers should ​go out for him because he has a lot on his mind today."

The family of the slain teacher, ​Lambert, said working at Silver Rail was a "dream job" for her.

"She always fought for ​the underdog and those with special needs," the family said in a statement that was read aloud at Friday's news conference.

Lambert's family also ‌praised Giamanco and expressed gratitude to him.

"We think he is a hero," ​the family said, according to the statement.

US school ​shootings have become more frequent in recent years. Since the start of this year, 118 people have been wounded or killed in 149 incidents involving a gun fired or brandished in a school, or gunshots striking school property, according to the K-12 School Shooting Database, a nonprofit online tracker.

A separate online database, the Gun Violence ​Archive, has recorded 371 mass shootings since January 2026, defining ‌mass shootings as four or more people being struck by gunfire, not including the shooter. Three of those, including the Bend incident, occurred in public schools, ​the archive said.

(Reporting by Herbert Villarraga and Deborah Bloom in Bend; Additional reproting by Jonathan Allen in New York and Steve Gorman in Los Angeles; ​Writing by Daniel Trotta; Editing by Paul Thomasch, Jonathan Spicer, Sergio Non and Cynthia Osterman)

Teacher tackled and fought Oregon school shooter

By Herbert Villarraga and Deborah Bloom

By Herbert Villarraga and Deborah Bloom

BEND, Oregon, Oct 16 (Reuters) - A teacher in the Oregon classroom where a shooter killed three children and an adult threw her cellphone at the shooter, tackled him and fought him in an act that saved lives, police said on Friday.

A day ‌into their investigation of the latest U.S. school shooting, authorities released new details of the scene inside a special needs classroom of Silver Rail ‌Elementary School where three school children aged 5, 8 and 11 and a teacher were killed by a 16-year-old former student.

Advertisement

Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz did not identify the teacher who fought the assailant, ​but told a press conference she threw her cell phone at the suspect, tackled him and fought to take his shotgun from him.

"She was not injured in that incident, but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed," Krantz said.

As the two wrestled, a parent entered the classroom and opened fire on the gunman, killing him.

Officials said the parent had followed the shooter into the school, upon witnessing him firing a shotgun from just outside campus. By the time police arrived within three minutes of receiving their first call, the shooter ‌was dead, police said.

In the meantime the 16-year-old assailant, who ⁠had shot through locked glass doors to enter campus, had killed four people and wounded two others.

Krantz, speaking to the heroism shown by the teacher who threw herself onto the suspect and the parent who shot him, said, "I don't think we can underestimate ⁠or under-appreciate that courage. When someone is willing to risk their own life for others, we recognize that."

He said that the bystander's actions "undoubtedly saved people," and "the teacher who was willing to stand and fight for her children, that's true heroism."

Krantz identified the shooter as Griffin J. John II, who was armed with 12-gauge shotgun. He fired about 15 rounds in the classroom ​and ​had another 44 rounds on him.

The parent who killed the shooter was identified as Kaylub Giamanco, his mother ​told the New York Times. She identified him as the ‌father of two girls who attend the school, according to video posted by the New York Times of Freeman reading a brief statement.

"He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support," Freeman said. "Kaylub's family, including his two daughters who attend the school, respectfully asks for privacy during this difficult time, and will not be participating in interviews at this time."

Residents of Bend, a city of about 100,000 people some 175 miles (280 km) southeast of Portland, gathered near the school to mourn on Friday morning, placing flowers and candles just outside yellow crime scene tape that cordoned off the ‌scene.

"Thank God for that father. He saved a lot of lives yesterday, and our prayers should ​go out for him because he has a lot on his mind today. We wish him well, ​and thank God for him," Michael Zappa, 71, who lives just blocks ​from the school, said through tears.

Brooke Olsen, the mother of a kindergartener who was safely reunited with her family after the shooting, ‌also expressed gratitude for the man who stopped the shooter.

"This is ​an extremely painful day of grief for ​everybody in Bend, especially Silver Rail families, and we have to think about what's next for safety measures."

Such school shootings have become common in the US, with each one reviving debates over gun laws in a country where a right to "keep and bear Arms" is protected under the Constitution's Second Amendment.

Some ​of the deadliest school attacks in the US include those ‌at Columbine High School in 1999, Sandy Hook Elementary School in 2012, Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in 2018 and Robb Elementary School in ​Uvalde, Texas, in 2022.

data.description:
California News
breaking

Wildfire races through SoCal, burning homes as mass evacuations ordered

By
Ross O'Keefe
Published Oct. 16, 2026, 1:06 p.m. PT

See more of our coverage in your search results.

A wildfire in Orange County exploded in size Friday, forcing evacuation orders as it torched homes and threatened dozens more, growing to over 460 acres in just three hours.

The Norte Fire broke out around 11:30 a.m. in the San Clemente area and quickly grew to at least 50 acres by around noon, according to the Orange County Fire Authority and CalFire.

By 1:12 p.m., the fire blew up to 250 acres and had 0% containment. The OCFA confirmed on X the blaze had “impacted” four homes off Via La Mira in San Juan Capistrano.

As of 2:41 p.m., the fire has burned 465 acres, according to CalFire.

Aerial footage from KTLA showed several homes burning in the San Clemente area as the fire approached many more.

“Crews are aggressively attacking the fire from the ground and air. Please continue to avoid the area,” Cal Fire wrote in a 12:30 p.m. update.

Evacuation orders have been issued for San Juan Zones 4, 5, and 10 as well as San Clemente Zones 12 and 13.

Heat, strong winds, and dry conditions were fueling the blaze as firefighters and aerial support worked to stop its spread.

Smoke from the fire prompted the Capistrano Unified School District to urge students to stay indoors due to the smoke.

San Clemente Mayor Rick Loeffler told KTLA the city had been making preparations for a fire.

“We actually instituted a goat program about a year ago, a pilot program to have goats start clearing our hillsides,” he said.

“The county supplied a pumpkin tank at the top of our ridge, which allows helicopters to come in and resupply their water quickly.”

The fire is one of several scorching SoCal right now, as fire officials are also dealing with the Bryson Fire in Malibu, the Henderson Fire near Camp Pendleton, and the Peak Fire in Azusa.

Ongoing Red Flag Warnings in effect across much of Los Angeles and Ventura counties have signalled ideal conditions for fires to break out.

Officials advise those in the community to avoid the area of the fire. There are no reported injuries. The cause of the fire is under investigation.

data.title: Trump suggests White House press secretary Katie Zacharia may be better off leaving
data.description:
Trump casts doubt on press secretary Zacharia's future

WILL WEISSERT and SEUNG MIN KIM
Updated Fri, October 16, 2026 at 5:21 PM UTC
1 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Trump

1 of 2
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia arrives with President Donald Trump at Glacier Park International Airport, Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, in Kalispell, Mont. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon) (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump signaled Friday that his embattled new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, may be on her way out — a mere week after he picked her for the post.

Speaking to reporters on the White House lawn as he left for a rally in Georgia, Trump said he'd spoken to Zacharia and that he felt she didn't deserve what he called negative media coverage.

Recounting what was said in that conversation, the president added, "I told her, 'I think you're better off being happy.'"

Advertisement

"We're talking about -- I want her to have a good life. I don't want her to have a life like she's led the last three days," Trump said.

He added, "I said, 'Katie, do you need this? I don't think you need this.'"

The president said he'd make a final determination later, perhaps after his campaign travel, adding, "When I get back, we're gonna talk."

He also said, "I told Katie, in my opinion, she was treated very unfairly."

Trump noted that Zacharia has been "brutalized by the media."

data.title: Amber Guyger released on parole after serving 7 years for Botham Jean’s murder
data.description:
Former Dallas police Officer Amber Guyger walked free from prison Friday morning after serving seven years behind bars for the murder of Botham Jean. 

Guyger, 38, shot 26-year-old Jean inside his apartment in September 2018. He had been sitting on his couch eating ice cream when Guyger, who was off-duty but still in uniform, opened the door. She said she mistook Jean’s apartment for her own and believed he was a burglar. He lived on the fourth floor; she lived on the third.

She was convicted of murder and sentenced to 10 years in prison in 2019, but was granted parole earlier this month. Guyger was released after 10 a.m. from the Christina Melton Crain Unit in Gatesville. CBS reported live from the unit, but news cameras didn’t capture her release. 

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Texas Department of Criminal Justice officials said Guyger was released into community supervision.

Guyger was required to travel directly to her new residence and check in immediately with her parole officer, according to Texas parole requirements. 

She was allowed to take home personal items accumulated while in prison and will either wear state-issued civilian clothes or clothes brought to her by visitors or the people picking her up. Guyger walked out with her parole papers, a temporary ID and a prepaid debit card or check for money left in her inmate trust account.

Guyger was denied parole in 2024 after the state parole board said she was not rehabilitated or ready for release. 

Her request was granted this time after a review found her record showed no documented pattern of violence, that she maintained a “satisfactory institutional adjustment” and that she completed a treatment plan that “should enhance” her chances of obtaining — and keeping — a full-time job, a Texas Board of Pardons and Paroles spokesperson said in early October. 

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The board has several options for what type of parole to grant an inmate, a vote that depends on individual circumstances and the inmate’s behavior during time served.

Guyger was granted direct release with no additional restrictions beyond her parole conditions, the least restrictive form of parole approval a Texas inmate can receive. 

The decision to release her sparked a new wave of interest and emotion around the case, which drew international attention, sparked protests and led Texas lawmakers to pass the Botham Jean Act.

Also known as Bo’s Law, the statute requires officers to keep their body cameras on for the entirety of their participation in an investigation. That same year, Dallas renamed part of South Lamar Street for Jean.

“The past eight years have been an incredibly traumatic and painful experience for Botham Jean’s family,” the family said in an official statement released in early October. “The loss of Botham has left our family forever dismembered, and that is something we continue to live with every day.” 

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Guyger’s parole conditions were not released, but her trial attorney, who no longer represents her, told The Dallas Morning News after the parole vote that she has a job that will keep her out of the public life and a living arrangement that will stay private. 

“She’s hopeful, optimistic, tremendously remorseful,” attorney Robert Rogers said. “That’s probably something she’ll always live with.”

Parole conditions

Most parolees must follow the same basic set of rules, alongside any special conditions decided by the parole board, which are typically kept confidential. 

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Guyger will have to follow her parole conditions until September 2029.

Failure to follow the conditions can result in parole revocation, which sends the inmate back to prison for the remainder of their sentence, or lesser sanctions such as curfew adjustments or brief incarceration in a facility designed for parolees.

State law requires all parolees to get permission from their parole officer if they want to change residences or leave the state. They must be working or in school, and they have to check in regularly with their parole officer, submit monthly education or work reports, and submit to random alcohol and drug testing and unannounced searches. 

They’re forbidden from breaking the law, owning or being around firearms and ammunition, and from contacting the victim directly or indirectly. They must make restitution payments and reimburse the prison for some educational programs.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Guyger still faces a judgment of nearly $100 million from a federal civil suit connected to Jean’s murder.
